interactions.title: Drive a process through its states
interactions.description: Send events in any order — admit, dispatch, time slice, I/O, exit — and watch the state change. Try the impossible ones too: each is explained.

interactions.title: CPU scheduling simulator
interactions.description: Edit the processes, pick an algorithm and step through every decision: the Gantt chart grows, the ready queue changes, and the last step shows CT, TAT, WT and RT.

interactions.title: Page replacement: FIFO, LRU and Optimal
interactions.description: Step through a reference string frame by frame, see each victim and why it was chosen, then compare all three policies — including with one more frame.

interactions.title: Banker's algorithm, check by check
interactions.description: Pick an example and, optionally, a request. Watch Need, the request checks and every Need ≤ Work test until the state is declared safe or unsafe.

interactions.title: Translate a logical address
interactions.description: Choose a page size, a page table and an address; split it into page and offset bits, look up the frame, and get the physical address — or a page fault.

interactions.title: Mutex or semaphore? Pick the tool

questions.prompt: Two threads update the same linked list. Each thread that locks the list will also unlock it. Which primitive fits best?
questions.explanation: This is mutual exclusion on shared data, and the same thread locks and unlocks — exactly what a mutex (with ownership) is for. A semaphore of 2 would let both threads in at once.

questions.prompt: A server has 10 database connections. A request thread should wait only when all 10 are in use. Which primitive fits best?
questions.explanation: A counting semaphore models N identical resources: each thread does wait() before taking a connection and signal() after returning it, so at most 10 are in use.

questions.prompt: A disk interrupt handler must wake a worker thread when new data has arrived. The handler never locked anything. What should it use?
options: Unlock a mutex owned by the worker
Signal a semaphore initialised to 0 that the worker waits on
questions.explanation: This is signalling between different threads. A mutex can only be unlocked by its owner, so the handler cannot use it; a semaphore has no owner, and starting at 0 makes the worker wait until the first signal.

questions.prompt: A code review finds an error path that calls signal(s) twice on a semaphore s = 1 used as a lock. What can happen?
options: Two threads can be inside the critical section at the same time
questions.explanation: A semaphore has no owner and simply counts: the extra signal leaves a spare permit, so two threads can pass wait(s) together and corrupt the shared data. A mutex would reject the unlock from a non-owner.

questions.prompt: A high-priority thread waits for a lock held by a low-priority thread while a medium-priority thread keeps running. Which primitive lets the OS fix this with priority inheritance?
options: A mutex, because it records its owner
questions.explanation: Priority inheritance needs to know whose priority to raise — the owner of the lock. Mutexes have owners; semaphores do not.

interactions.title: Final check: OS interview essentials
interactions.description: Ten mixed questions across the whole subject — the traps interviewers like most.

questions.prompt: A process blocked on a disk read is told the read has finished. Which state does it move to?
questions.explanation: An event completion moves a process from Waiting to Ready; it runs again only when the scheduler dispatches it. There is no Waiting → Running transition.

questions.prompt: Which statement about threads of the same process is correct?
options: Each thread has its own heap
Threads share the stack but not the heap
Each thread has its own stack; the heap is shared
questions.explanation: Threads share code, global data, the heap and open files; each has its own stack, registers and program counter.

questions.prompt: A program calls getpid(), which returns immediately. What happens?
options: A mode switch into the kernel and back, with no context switch
Nothing — getpid runs entirely in user mode on every system
questions.explanation: A system call is a mode switch. A context switch happens only if the call blocks or the scheduler chooses another process.

questions.prompt: P1 (AT 0, BT 4), P2 (AT 1, BT 3), P3 (AT 2, BT 1), P4 (AT 3, BT 2). What is the average waiting time under FCFS?
questions.explanation: Gantt P1 0–4, P2 4–7, P3 7–8, P4 8–10. Waiting times 0, 3, 5, 5 → 13 ÷ 4 = 3.25. (5.75 is the average turnaround time.)

questions.prompt: Which scheduling algorithms can never starve a process?
questions.explanation: In FCFS and Round Robin every process eventually reaches the head of the queue. SJF, SRTF and priority scheduling can pass a process over indefinitely unless aging is added.

questions.prompt: Why is count++ on a shared variable not thread-safe?
options: It is a single instruction that the CPU cannot interrupt
It is a load, an add and a store that another thread can interleave
Java forbids it on shared variables
It always runs in kernel mode
questions.explanation: Two threads can both load the same value before either stores, so one increment is lost. That is a race condition.

questions.prompt: All four Coffman conditions hold in a system with multiple instances of each resource. Is it deadlocked?
options: Not necessarily — the conditions are necessary, not sufficient
Only if the system is unsafe
questions.explanation: The four conditions must all hold for a deadlock, but their presence does not guarantee one; with several instances a process outside the cycle may release a resource and break it.

questions.prompt: Page size is 1 KB and page 2 is in frame 7. What is the physical address of logical address 3000?
Which page-replacement algorithm can show Belady's anomaly?
questions.explanation: FIFO can produce more faults with more frames (9 → 10 on 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5). LRU and Optimal are stack algorithms and never do.

questions.prompt: During thrashing, what does CPU utilisation typically do?
options: It falls, because processes wait for paging I/O
It depends only on the scheduling algorithm
questions.explanation: Processes spend their time blocked on page faults, so the CPU has little to run. Adding processes makes it worse; the fix is to reduce the degree of multiprogramming or add memory.

interactions.title: OS flashcards: the must-know definitions
interactions.description: Twenty cards covering the most asked Operating Systems definitions and differences.

cards.back: Software between hardware and programs: it manages CPU, memory, storage and devices, and provides services such as processes and files.
Restricted vs privileged CPU mode. Programs enter the kernel only through a system call, an interrupt or an exception.
A controlled request from a user program to the kernel, made with a trap instruction and dispatched through the system-call table.
A program is a passive file; a process is a program in execution with its own memory, registers and state.
New, Ready, Running, Waiting (Blocked), Terminated. Waiting → Ready when the event completes, never straight to Running.
The kernel's record of a process: PID, state, saved registers and PC, scheduling data, memory information, open files.
Saving the running process's CPU state into its PCB and loading another's. Pure overhead; thread switches are cheaper than process switches.
A process has its own address space; threads share their process's code, data, heap and files but each has its own stack and registers.
Preemptive: the OS can take the CPU away (SRTF, RR). Non-preemptive: the process keeps it until it blocks or ends (FCFS, SJF).
TAT = CT − AT. WT = TAT − BT. RT = first start − AT.

cards.front: Round Robin quantum too large / too small
cards.back: Too large: behaves like FCFS. Too small: context-switch overhead dominates.
A ready process is passed over indefinitely (SJF, SRTF, priority). Fix: aging — raise its priority as it waits.
A result that depends on the timing of unsynchronised concurrent access to shared data with at least one write (e.g. count++).
Mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.
Mutex: a lock with an owner, one holder. Semaphore: a counter with wait/signal, no owner, up to N holders or used for signalling.
Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait — all four are necessary.
Need = Max − Allocation. Grant a request only if, after pretending to grant it, a safe sequence still exists.
p = address ÷ page size, d = address mod page size; physical address = frame × page size + d.
An access to a valid page that is not in RAM: trap, load the page from disk, update the page table, restart the instruction.
The system spends more time paging than executing because the working sets exceed RAM; CPU utilisation drops.
